title: Where prayer comes from (CCC 2652–2660)
hook: the word, the liturgy, faith, hope, charity, and today

segments.voice: Yesterday, five forms: blessing, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise. Your line was five ways to speak. Which of the five came easiest when you tried them? Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

Turn on a kitchen tap and water comes out. Simple. Except the water didn't start in the kitchen. Somewhere out of sight there's a reservoir, a main under the street, a pipe in the wall, and pressure pushing the whole way. The tap is only where it shows up. The Catechism asks the same kind of question about prayer. If prayer is speaking with God, where does the speaking come from? Not out of nowhere, it says. It names a handful of springs. And the last spring on its list is the plainest one of all, so plain it's easy to miss. Today: where prayer comes from.
screen: `A TAP IN THE KITCHEN.` → `THE WATER STARTS ELSEWHERE.` → `WHERE DOES PRAYER START?`

segments.voice: The Catechism begins back at the well from a few days ago, with the promise Jesus makes there: the water he gives, in the Douay-Rheims wording, "shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting." The Catechism reads that living water as the Holy Spirit, and then asks where we go to draw it. First spring: the word of God. It recalls a line from Saint Ambrose: when we pray, we speak to God, and when we read the scriptures, we hear him. Reading and praying are two halves of one conversation. Second spring: the liturgy. The Mass and the Church's daily prayer are where the Church prays together, and the Catechism describes personal prayer taking that liturgy in and making it its own, during the celebration and after it. Third: three virtues. Faith, which it calls the way in. Hope, in Paul's words: "hope confoundeth not: because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts." And charity, love itself. Then the surprise. The last spring isn't a book or a building. It's today. The Catechism points to a psalm: "To day if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts." We learn to pray at certain moments, it says, but the Spirit is offered at all times, in the events of each day. A traffic jam. A waiting room. A child's question over cereal. In this reading, those aren't interruptions of prayer. They're where it can spring up.
screen: `THE WORD OF GOD.` · `THE LITURGY.` · `FAITH, HOPE, CHARITY.` · `TODAY IS A SPRING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray from this moment. Settle, and breathe. Don't reach for a holy thought. Look at what's actually here. The chair under you. The sound in the next room. The thing on your mind for later this afternoon. Pick one of them. If you pray, you can bring that one thing to God just as it is, in a sentence of your own. If you don't, simply let it be noticed, fully, without fixing it. The bell holds the time.
Where prayer comes from. In the Catechism, the springs prayer draws on: the word of God, the liturgy, faith, hope and charity, and today itself. Today's words.
Your line: today is a source. Today, when something ordinary interrupts you, a call, a delay, a kindness, try treating it as a place prayer could start. Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics draw their prayer from reading scripture, from the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, and from the events of an ordinary day, which some bring to God as they happen.
